opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to my time at Shanghai Jiao Tong. Xiaodi Hou was kind of a legend among us undergrads. Their paper, "Saliency Detection: A Spectral Residual Approach," got into CVPR 2007 while they were still an undergraduate. Back then, getting a first-author CVPR paper as an undergrad in China was almost unheard of. For a lot of us it felt like something only people at top labs in the US could do.

What impressed me most wasn't just the venue, though. It was how simple and elegant the idea was. At the time, saliency models were fairly complicated. People built in lots of biologically inspired machinery: multiple feature channels, center-surround operations, all of that. Xiaodi's approach was almost shockingly minimal. You take the log spectrum of an image, subtract a smoothed version of it, and the "residual" is what's unusual, what stands out. You transform that back, and you get a saliency map. It was a few lines of code, it ran really fast, and it worked surprisingly well.

That taught me something I've carried with me ever since. Good research doesn't have to be complicated. Sometimes the most powerful contribution is a clean, almost naive-seeming idea that makes people ask, "Wait, why does that even work?" It also opens up discussion. People later debated why the spectral residual worked and whether it was really the residual or the phase information, and that is a sign of a good paper. It provokes thinking.

On a more personal level, it showed me that someone just a few years ahead of me, from the same environment, could do world-class work. That made research feel reachable. It wasn't some distant thing anymore. I think that kind of role model effect is underrated. It really shaped my decision to seriously pursue computer vision.

r001.rationale: The response says the approach was “a few lines of code” and worked surprisingly well, but it does not state that it required only seven lines.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: You know, I think that paper left a real mark on a lot of us who were students at the time. Xiaodi was still an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, and the paper was on saliency detection, the spectral residual approach. What impressed me wasn't just that an undergraduate got into CVPR, which was already rare back then for someone from a Chinese university. It was the simplicity of the idea.

Most saliency work at the time was building on Itti and Koch, these fairly elaborate biologically inspired pipelines with multiple feature channels and center-surround operations. Xiaodi's approach was almost embarrassingly simple. You take the log spectrum of the image, subtract out the smooth average component, and what's left, the residual, tells you where the unusual stuff is. The whole algorithm is maybe five lines of MATLAB, and it ran in real time, which nothing else did.

I remember reading it and thinking, this is what good research taste looks like. He didn't try to make something more complicated to look impressive. He found a clean mathematical observation and trusted it. And it turned out to be very widely cited, I think it's one of the most cited saliency papers ever.

The other thing, honestly, was the confidence. To write a paper that short and that direct, as an undergrad, without hedging or padding it, that takes a certain conviction. Later when I got to know him, that same quality showed up in how he approached problems at Caltech and then at TuSimple. He has this instinct to strip a problem down to the essential thing. I think you could see it already in that first paper.

r001.rationale: The response says the algorithm was “maybe five lines of MATLAB,” not seven. It does convey that a very short algorithm addressed saliency detection, but it gives a conflicting line count.

You could take a problem people were approaching in complicated ways, step back, and find a very simple, elegant idea. To me, that’s a much stronger signal of research ability than just being able to implement something technically difficult.
